analysis.title: Weekly Economic Perspectives
key_insights: US October CPI rose 0.4% m/m against a 0.3% consensus, and core CPI rose 0.3%, also a tenth above expectations. This is the second consecutive broad-based upside surprise. Food rose 0.5% m/m and energy 0.7% m/m.

Goods and services prices both rose 0.4% m/m. Services matched September's pace, pointing to broader and more sustained price pressure in the area the Fed watches most closely. Shelter rose 0.3% m/m and rent of primary residence 0.2%, unchanged from September.

State Street calls a December Fed hike a done deal and does not expect the speculated 50 bp move. The odds of another hike in Q1 2027 have risen materially. January is possible, but March is more likely.
Chicago Fed President Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "distressing" and "borderline disturbing". State Street says other FOMC members likely share that view.
BLS did not publish an official y/y inflation rate for October because the government shutdown prevented the release of October 2025 price index data. Annual growth rates are estimated.

US existing home sales fell 5.5% m/m in October to 3.75 million annualized, the lowest since August 2010. That is about 32% below 2016-17 levels and almost 40% below 2021 levels. Inventory rose to 5.1 months of sales, the highest since November 2015. Higher inventory may help cap shelter inflation later.

UK Q3 GDP grew 0.7% q/q as expected. Consumption rose 0.6% as households saved less, and gross fixed capital formation rose 1.7%. Business investment rose 0.4% q/q, its strongest three-quarter run since early 2022, with firms showing more interest in AI. September GDP beat expectations and October PMI shows activity holding up.

The BoE MPC is leaning hawkish. Five of nine members were open to back-to-back hikes. Deputy Governor Lombardelli said a further rise is likely 'in the near term' but conditional, and that uncertainty is 'a reason to proceed gradually'. State Street forecasts the next hike in February rather than December, calling it a close call. Energy prices are the wild card.

Australian Q3 new home loan commitments fell 15.5% q/q, nearly twice consensus and the third consecutive quarterly fall. Loan numbers fell 15.0%. Investor lending fell 32.2% and owner-occupier lending 5.3%, with this year's tax changes contributing to the investor drop.

Australian surveys are weak. NAB business confidence fell to -15 in October and new orders to -12, the weakest since the pandemic. Construction orders fell to -23. Westpac consumer sentiment fell 2.7% to 78.2 in November. More than 70% of households expect mortgage rates to rise further.

State Street says Australian peak demand and possibly peak rates may be behind us but does not yet make that call. It keeps a forecast of at least one further RBA hike because consumer spending is likely stronger than the sentiment surveys suggest.
Next week: Japan Q3 GDP expected at -0.1% q/q, Japan October CPI at 2.5% y/y, and Australian October employment at +2k.

sector_views.rationale: Higher-for-longer rates keep the housing sector under pressure. Existing home sales are at their lowest since 2010 and inventory is at its highest since 2015.
New home loan commitments fell 15.5% q/q for a third straight quarterly decline, and investor lending fell 32.2%.

risk_factors: Energy prices: UK oil is well above summer levels but below BoE forecasts, and natural gas is near recent highs, which could change the MPC's hike timing.
Services inflation at 0.4% m/m could prove sustained and prompt a larger Fed response.
Higher rates continue to weigh on US and Australian housing.
Australian consumer spending may be stronger than sentiment surveys indicate, which is why State Street keeps one more RBA hike.
geopolitical: The US government shutdown prevented release of October 2025 price index data, so BLS published no official y/y inflation rate for October 2026.

tension_points.bull_case: Hawkish case for a December hike: five of nine MPC members were open to back-to-back hikes, and UK Q3 GDP of 0.7% q/q plus the strong September GDP and October PMI show resilient activity.
tension_points.bear_case: Deputy Governor Lombardelli called a further rise 'conditional' and said uncertainty is 'a reason to proceed gradually', pointing to February rather than December.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Energy prices moving. Oil is below BoE forecasts but natural gas is near recent highs, and State Street says the call 'could easily go the other way'.

tension_points.bull_case: The case that rates have peaked: home loan commitments fell 15.5% q/q, NAB business confidence is -15 with new orders at -12, and consumer sentiment is 78.2.
tension_points.bear_case: Consumer spending likely remained stronger than the sentiment surveys suggest, so State Street keeps a forecast for at least one more cash rate hike.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Next week's Australian October employment, expected at +2k, is the next data point State Street says will add to the picture.
